questions.question_text: If $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ and $I=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{aligned}],$ then which one of the following holds for all $n \ge 1,$ by the principle of mathematical induction?
questions.question_html: If $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ and $I=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{aligned}],$ then which one of the following holds for all $n \ge 1,$ by the principle of mathematical induction?
questions.explanation_text: Given $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ $\therefore$ $A \times A$ = $A^{2}$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ and $A^{3}$ = $A^{2} \times A$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{aligned}]$ So we can say $A^{n}$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ n & 1 \end{aligned}]$ Now $nA-(n-1)I$ = $[\begin{aligned} n & 0 \\ n & n \end{aligned}]$ - $[\begin{aligned} n-1 & 0 \\ 0 & n-1 \end{aligned}]$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ n & 1 \end{aligned}]$ = $A^{n}$ $\therefore$ $A^{n}=nA-(n-1)I$
questions.explanation_html:
Given $A=[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{aligned}]$

$\therefore$ $A \times A$ = $A^{2}$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{aligned}]$

and $A^{3}$ = $A^{2} \times A$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 \end{aligned}]$

So we can say $A^{n}$ = $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ n & 1 \end{aligned}]$

Now $nA-(n-1)I$

= $[\begin{aligned} n & 0 \\ n & n \end{aligned}]$ - $[\begin{aligned} n-1 & 0 \\ 0 & n-1 \end{aligned}]$

= $[\begin{aligned} 1 & 0 \\ n & 1 \end{aligned}]$ = $A^{n}$

$\therefore$ $A^{n}=nA-(n-1)I$

questions.question_text: Let $S(K)$ $=1+3+5...+(2K-1)=3+K^{2}.$ Then which of the following is true
questions.question_html: Let $S(K)$ $=1+3+5...+(2K-1)=3+K^{2}.$ Then which of the following is true

options.label: A
options.text: Principle of mathematical induction can be used to prove the formula
options.html: Principle of mathematical induction can be used to prove the formula

options.label: D
options.html: $S(1)$ is correct

questions.explanation_text: Given $S(K)$ $=1+3+5...+(2K-1)=3+K^{2}$ When k = 1, S(1): 1 = 3 + 1, L.H.S of S(k) $\ne$ R.H.S of S(k) So S(1) is not true. As S(1) is not true so principle of mathematical induction can not be used. S(K+1) = 1 + 3 + 5... + (2K - 1) + (2K + 1) = 3 + (k + 1) 2 Now let S(k) is true $\therefore$ 1 + 3 + 5 +........(2k - 1) = 3 + k 2 $\Rightarrow$ 1 + 3 + 5 +........(2k - 1) + (2k + 1) = 3 + k 2 + 2k +1 = 3 + (k + 1) 2 $\Rightarrow$ S(k + 1) is true. $\therefore$ S(k) $\Rightarrow$ S(k + 1)
questions.explanation_html:
Given $S(K)$ $=1+3+5...+(2K-1)=3+K^{2}$

When k = 1, S(1): 1 = 3 + 1,

L.H.S of S(k) $\ne$ R.H.S of S(k)

So S(1) is not true.

As S(1) is not true so principle of mathematical induction can not be used.

S(K+1) = 1 + 3 + 5... + (2K - 1) + (2K + 1) = 3 + (k + 1)2

Now let S(k) is true

$\therefore$ 1 + 3 + 5 +........(2k - 1) = 3 + k2

$\Rightarrow$ 1 + 3 + 5 +........(2k - 1) + (2k + 1) = 3 + k2 + 2k +1

= 3 + (k + 1)2

$\Rightarrow$ S(k + 1) is true.

$\therefore$ S(k) $\Rightarrow$ S(k + 1)

questions.question_text: If $a_{n}=\sqrt{7+\sqrt{7+\sqrt{7+.......}}}$ having $n$ radical signs then by methods of mathematical induction which is true
questions.question_html: If $a_{n}=\sqrt{7+\sqrt{7+\sqrt{7+.......}}}$ having $n$ radical signs then by methods of mathematical induction which is true
questions.explanation_html:
Given $a_{n}=\sqrt{7+\sqrt{7+\sqrt{7+.......}}}$

$\therefore$ $a_{n}=\sqrt{7+a_{n}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $a_{n}^{2}=7+a_{n}$

$\Rightarrow$ $a_{n}^{2}-a_{n}-7=0$

$\Rightarrow a_{n}=\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1-4 \times 1 \times -7}}{2}$

$\Rightarrow a_{n}=\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{29}}{2}$

As $a_{n}$ > 0,

$\therefore$ $a_{n}=\frac{1+\sqrt{29}}{2}$ = 3.19

So $a_{n}>3∀n \ge 1$
